=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-23 PD/STF-PIA-23-2.docx ===
STF-PIA-23-2

Question: 

Does Georgia Power currently calculate an aggregate system utilization figure (energy delivered divided by available capacity) for generation, transmission, and distribution? If so- please provide the details.

Response:

Please see the Company’s response to STF-PIA-23-1 for transmission and distribution.

The Company does not calculate an aggregate system utilization figure for generation. As a member of the Southern Company Pool, the Company’s load obligations are pooled with the other participating pool member loads and their generating resources are dispatched in the most economical manner possible to reliably serve all pooled loads, regardless of ownership. Also, generation utilization is not a meaningful standalone metric because different resource types serve different functions. For example, peaking units are designed to run infrequently and provide reliability during periods of highest demand. Low utilization for these resources is expected and does not indicate inefficiency or ineffective operation.







=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-23 PD/STF-PIA-23-6.docx ===
STF-PIA-23-6

Question: 

Do any DSM/energy-efficiency programs get credited toward reducing system peak demand in a way that shows up in the reserve margin or IRP planning numbers?

Response:

In IRP planning numbers, the Company considers cost-effective energy efficiency and demand response programs as priority resources. These programs are the first resources considered in serving customers’ future needs and are included in the planning process prior to identifying the need for any new supply-side resources.  

Energy efficiency programs reduce the Company’s load forecast directly. Their projected energy and demand savings are embedded in the forecast used for planning. Demand response measures, by contrast, are treated as a capacity resource and are included in the resource ledger under Dispatchable Demand-Side Options (“DSOs”), as consistently demonstrated in all of the Company’s filed workpapers and models in IRPs and resource certification filings.

Both the load forecast (reflecting energy efficiency savings) and the capacity resource ledger (reflecting demand response capacity) feed into the reserve margin study. Energy efficiency reduces the peak demand the reserve margin is measured against, while demand response adds capacity that counts toward meeting it.




=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-23 PD/STF-PIA-23-9.docx ===
STF-PIA-23-9

Question: 

Some recent studies show that flexible resources may be good options for large load by the use of existing headroom plus flexible resources plus phased investment and then build permanent infrastructure as load becomes more certain. In other words, build less first and keep options open. For example: use of battery, demand response, flexible interconnection, managed load, and use of grid enhancing technologies. Use these flexible resources until load becomes sufficiently certain to justify the permanent investment. However, they may also require major transmission upgrades because of fundamental thermal or stability constraints. For example, A 100 MW battery cannot simply replace 1000 MW transmission investment. Therefore, when large load project is uncertain or phased, has Georgia Power evaluated flexible interconnection, storage, demand response, managed load, and grid- enhancing technologies etc. as an interim solution to reduce the risk of building infrastructure that could later be underutilized? If yes, please explain the details. If no, please explain why Georgia Power has not evaluated such options.

Response:

As discussed in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Volume 3, transmission capacity is determined by transmission system evaluations using a measured approach that balances safety, reliability, affordability, and resiliency.
 
Consistent with that approach, the Company plans and builds for firm and future firm load commitments. The Company is not building infrastructure to accommodate non-committed large load growth, as doing so could result in unnecessary costs being borne by customers.

Under the Commission-approved rules and regulations for large load customers, the Commission and the Company protect existing customers from bearing any of the costs of adding large load customers. Contract provisions such as minimum term lengths, minimum bills, performance security, and termination schedules ensure large load customers cover all costs necessary to serve their load, including upstream transmission system enhancements and infrastructure investments. In addition, through existing cost recovery mechanisms such as upfront payments, large load customers are responsible for all the costs of the local infrastructure required to serve their load.

The Company’s measured approach also includes customer-specific flexibility options designed to support system safety, reliability, affordability, and resiliency while accommodating for economic development growth in a responsible manner. See the Company’s load flexibility Compliance Report filed with the Commission on June 30, 2026, in Docket Nos. 56298 & 56310.

For additional information regarding grid-enhancing technologies, see Section 11.4 Innovative Solutions in the Company’s 2025 IRP Main Document in Docket Nos. 56002 & 56003.

STF-PIA-23-3

Question: 

Given that Georgia Power already maintains a target reserve margin above the industry standard of ~15%, can some of that existing transmission capacity headroom be used more efficiently to serve uncertain large-load growth before additional infrastructure is built, and if so, how much new large-load demand could that reserve margin accommodate before triggering new transmission investment?

Response:

The reference to 15% as the industry-standard target reserve margin is inaccurate. In its reliability assessments, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) compares each assessment area against the reference margin level set by that area’s state regulator, independent system operator/regional transmission organization, or other authority and applies 15% only as a default for predominantly thermal areas that do not provide one, which is the case for the Southeastern Subregion of SERC Reliability Corporation (SERC). The Company’s Commission-approved target reserve margins are set through a comprehensive reserve margin study specifically for the Southern Company System and are not comparable to NERC’s 15% reference margin  for reliability assessments.

Importantly, “transmission capacity headroom” and target reserve margin are two distinct and separate concepts. The target reserve margin is maintained to ensure generation resource-adequacy, while the transmission adequacy analysis, as described in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Volume 3, addresses a different purpose. That analysis ensures reliable delivery of energy from generation resources to loads under various planning events and ensures compliance with mandatory NERC reliability standards. 

The Company’s transmission planning process and methodologies are described in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix, Volume 3. This document includes information regarding transmission planning principles, transmission system evaluation, planning coordination, project development and evaluation, planning tools, planning guidelines, applicable NERC reliability standards, and other considerations used in developing the Ten-Year Plan. The ability to serve new large loads depends on a variety of factors, including the location, timing, and load profile of the customer under contract, as well as the generation, transmission, distribution, and interconnection facilities necessary to reliably serve all customers. Please refer to the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix, Volume 3, for a complete discussion of these topics.

=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-23 PD/STF-PIA-23-1.docx ===
STF-PIA-23-1

Question: 

Does Georgia Power currently track grid utilization metrics at the transmission, substation, and distribution level? If so, please identify the metrics and provide a brief description of each. If not, what information would be needed to develop such metrics?

Response:

In general, the Company interprets the broad industry definition of grid utilization as a measure of how much available capacity is being used by comparing facility loading to the applicable facility rating. The Company evaluates utilization based on usable capacity under defined operating and reliability conditions across the transmission, substation, and distribution systems as part of its planning processes to identify and understand loading trends, evaluate future system needs, and determine when facilities may approach planning or operational limitations.  

Examples of grid utilization assessments performed include:

Transmission: Evaluation of loading on transmission facilities, such as transmission lines and bulk power transformers, relative to applicable ratings under normal operating and contingency scenarios across multiple seasons.

Substation: Evaluation of loading on substation facilities, such as load-serving power transformers, relative to applicable ratings under normal operating scenarios across multiple seasons.

Distribution: Evaluation of loading on distribution facilities, such as distribution feeders, relative to applicable ratings under normal operating scenarios across multiple seasons.

The Company’s transmission planning methodologies and guidelines are described in Sections A and B of Technical Appendix Volume 3 in the 2025 IRP in Docket No. 56002.  For load-serving substations and distribution feeders, the Company uses internal planning criteria to evaluate projected peak loads against facility ratings to maintain safe and reliable electric service to its customers. 

While utilization assessments are considered as part of the Company’s planning process, utilization is viewed alongside other inputs including safety, reliability, resilience, operational flexibility, and affordability. The Company seeks to make efficient use of existing facilities and does not rely on a single, standalone grid utilization metric when identifying and evaluating system needs.

Question: 

Does the Large Load Economic Development Report show where (which substations or transmission zones) new load is expected to connect, so staff can judge whether it lands in areas with spare capacity?

Response:

The Large Load Economic Development Report provides the city, county, and GPS coordinates for all committed and potential large load projects. This report is not intended to provide power delivery-related information. The Georgia Power Company Annual Transmission Update Report, the latest of which was filed with the Commission on February 27, 2026, provides power delivery-related information.

Furthermore, as discussed in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Volume 3, transmission capacity is determined by transmission system evaluations. The ability to serve new large loads depends on a variety of factors, including the location, timing, and load profile of the customer under contract, as well as the generation, transmission, distribution, and interconnection facilities necessary to reliably serve all customers.

=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-23 PD/STF-PIA-23-7.docx ===
STF-PIA-23-7

Question: 

How does SAIDI/SAIFI performance get weighed against utilization goals — is there a risk that running assets harder to raise utilization could work against the reliability metrics Georgia Power is already held to?

Response:

Adopting broad grid utilization metrics with goals to increase said metrics would create unnecessary risk to reliability performance and overall customer experience. Such risks include reduced equipment life, longer outage times, and diminished customer value taken from the Company’s longstanding smart grid investments. 
For example, if every feeder operated at or near its full capacity all the time, the system would not have the capacity to manage reliability events. If an outage impacted a portion of one circuit, neighboring circuits could not take on the affected load because the system is already at full capacity. Customers would then face longer outages and lower reliability, impacting SAIDI/SAIFI, and safety may also be at risk. Operational flexibility is intentional because it allows the system to respond when problems occur. 
Georgia Power has practices and work processes across multiple workgroups to mitigate risks related to asset loading and grid configuration. The Company does not operate equipment outside of rated capabilities or historical best practices to meet any particular metric. The Company works to improve SAIDI and SAIFI performance metrics by operating the system efficiently and pursuing system improvements that deliver greater value to customers.

After a non-wires alternative or grid-enhancing technology is approved, how will Georgia Power measure actual performance and determine whether the expected capital cost or reliability benefit was achieved?

Response:
